rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iyyā takes attached first, second, or third person pronouns and forms an independent accusative pronoun, not an overt noun with an annexed suffix, contrary to an unnamed claimant.
rows.anchor: فيكون ضمير نصب منفصلاً لا اسماً ظاهراً أضيف خلافاً لزاعمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Grammarians differ over whether the pronoun is the whole form or only part of it, whether the suffixes are letters or nouns, and whether iyyā is added solely to host pronouns.
rows.anchor: وهل الضمير هو مع لواحقه أو هو وحده

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read iyyā with a kasra on hamza and a doubled yāʾ.
rows.anchor: وأما لغاته فبكسر الهمزة وتشديد الياء

rows.speaker: الفضل الرقاشي
rows.claim: Al-Faḍl al-Ruqāshī reads it with a fatḥa on hamza and a doubled yāʾ.
rows.anchor: وبفتح الهمزة وتشديد الياء ، وبها قرأ الفضل الرقاشي

rows.speaker: عمرو بن فائد
rows.claim: ʿAmr ibn Fāʾid, transmitting from Ubayy, reads it with kasra on hamza and an undoubled yāʾ.
rows.anchor: وبها قرأ عمرو بن فائد

rows.speaker: ابن السوار الغنوي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Sawwār al-Ghanawī reads the forms with either a kasra or fatḥa hamza replaced by hāʾ.
rows.anchor: وبذلك قرأ ابن السوار الغنوي

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda’s derivation of iyyā is weak; Abū Ḥayyān says he was poor at grammar despite mastery of lexicon and Arab history.
rows.anchor: وكان أبو عبيدة لا يحسن النحو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If iyyā is derived, proposed sources include the word in a poetic line and āya, with the latter analysis making its root consonant yāʾ.
rows.anchor: فا ولذكراها إذا ما ذكرتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Several competing root and pattern analyses are proposed for iyyā, but Abū Ḥayyān judges them all weak.
rows.anchor: وهل وزنه إفعل وأصله إ أو و أو إ أو ي أو فعيل فأصله أو يو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Annexing iyyā to an overt noun is rare, or a poetic necessity; the text gives examples of both.
rows.anchor: نحو : دعني وإيا خالد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the familiar warning use, iyyā can contain a nominative pronoun that is followed by a nominative emphatic pronoun.
rows.anchor: واستعماله تحذيراً معروف فيحتمل ضميراً مرفوعاً

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority explain worship as humility and submission, which Abū Ḥayyān later identifies as the basic lexical sense.
rows.anchor: العبادة : التذلل ، قاله الجمهور

rows.speaker: ابن السكيت
rows.claim: Ibn al-Sikkīt gives tajrīd, stripping or devotion, as an alternative meaning of worship.
rows.anchor: أو التجريد ، قاله ابن السكيت ، وتعديه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The transitive sense changes with form: ʿabadt al-rajul means I humbled the man, while ʿabadt Allāh means I humbled myself to God.
rows.anchor: عبدت الرجل ذللته ، وعبدت الله ذللت له

rows.speaker: الحسن، وأبو مجلز، وأبو المتوكل
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan, Abū Majliz, and Abū al-Mutawakkil read iyyāka yaʿbudu with yāʾ and a passive verb.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن ، وأبو مجلز ، وأبو المتوكل

rows.speaker: بعض أهل مكة
rows.claim: Some Meccans read naʿbud with the dāl unvowelled.
rows.anchor: وعن بعض أهل مكة نعبد بإسكان الدال

rows.speaker: زيد بن علي، ويحيى بن وثاب، وعبيد بن عمير الليثي
rows.claim: Zayd ibn ʿAlī, Yaḥyā ibn Waththāb, and ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr al-Laythī read naʿbud with kasra on its initial nūn.
rows.anchor: وقرأ زيد بن علي ، ويحيى بن وثاب ، وعبيد بن عمير الليثي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Istiʿāna means seeking aid; the form istifʿala has twelve uses, including request, transformation, treating something as something, and several forms of equivalence or substitution.
rows.anchor: والطلب أحد معاني استفعل

rows.speaker: صاحب اللوامح
rows.claim: The author of al-Lawāmiʿ reports a form wayyāka, with hamza changed to wāw, but is unsure whether it came from al-Farrāʾ or Arab usage.
rows.anchor: وقال صاحب اللوامح : وقد جاء فيه وياك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The change to wāw reflects aversion to hamza; this reverses the alternative tendency to replace a kasra-bearing wāw with hamza.
rows.anchor: وفي وياك فروا من الهمزة إلى الواو

rows.speaker: أبو الحسن بن سيده
rows.claim: Ibn Sīda says tamāsaktu, masaktu, amsaktu, and istamsaktu bi-shayʾ have the same sense, holding fast to something; this adds two equivalence uses to istifʿala.
rows.anchor: أبو الحسن بن سيده في المحكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Istiʿāna means asking for help, as in other verbs of request.
rows.anchor: فاستعان طلب العون ، كاستغفر

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority pronounce the initial nūn of nastaʿīn with fatḥa, the Hijazi and most correct form.
rows.anchor: وفتح نون نستعين قرأ بها الجمهور

rows.speaker: عبيد بن عمير الليثي، وزر بن حبيش، ويحيى بن وثاب، والنخعي، والأعمش
rows.claim: These readers pronounce the initial nūn of nastaʿīn with kasra, matching Qays, Tamīm, Asad, and Rabīʿa; similar imperfect forms follow the same rule.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عبيد بن عمير الليثي ، وزر بن حبيش

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر الطوسي
rows.claim: Abū Jaʿfar al-Ṭūsī identifies the kasra on the initial nūn as the dialect of Hudhayl.
rows.anchor: أبو جعفر الطوسي : هي لغة هذيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In these forms wāw shifts to alif in istaʿāna and mustaʿān, and to yāʾ in nastaʿīn and mustaʿīn; deletion in istiʿāna belongs to morphology.
rows.anchor: وانقلاب الواو ألفاً في استعان ومستعان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Istaʿāna can take a direct object or the preposition bi-; its verbal noun also shows morphological deletion.
rows.anchor: ويعدى استعان بنفسه وبالباء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iyyāka is the fronted direct object of naʿbud.
rows.anchor: إياك مفعول مقدم ، والزمخشري يزعم

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī takes object fronting to mean exclusivity, as though the verse said only you we worship; Abū Ḥayyān says it instead signals care and attention to the object.
rows.anchor: والزمخشري يزعم أنه لا يقدم على العامل إلا للتخصيص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An Arab addressed an insulter with iyyāka aʿnī; the reply wa-ʿanka aʿriḍ shows that speakers front what matters most.
rows.anchor: وسب أعرابي آخر فأعرض عنه وقال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iyyāka is an iltifāt from third-person reference, since a consistent third-person construction would say iyyāhu.
rows.anchor: وإياك التفات لأنه انتقال من الغيبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iltifāt shifts among third person, address, and first person, in any direction; the same referent must remain in view, whether named or pronominal.
rows.anchor: والانتقال من فنون البلاغة ، وهو الانتقال من الغيبة للخطاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rhetoricians cite iltifāt as a display of command over expression; some also seek a distinct local effect, and Ibn al-Athīr wrote notably on the device.
rows.anchor: فائدة هذا الالتفات إظهار الملكة في الكلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After praising God for lordship, mercy, and kingship in 1:2–4, the speaker turns to address Him and says that he and others worship and submit to Him.
rows.anchor: أقبل الحامد مخبراً بأثر ذكره الحمد المستقر له منه ومن غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first-person plural nūn includes the speaker and others, just as the preceding praise encompasses all who praise.
rows.anchor: وكذلك أتى بالنون التي تكون له ولغيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Addressing a present person directly is more tactful and effective than referring to him as absent with iyyāhu.
rows.anchor: ونظير هذا أنك تذكر شخصاً متصفاً بأوصاف جليلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The direct address in iyyāka naʿbud is a preparation for the supplication ihdinā that follows.
rows.anchor: ولأنه ذكر ذلك توطئة للدعاء في قوله اهدنا

rows.speaker: من ذهب إلى أن ملك منادى
rows.claim: If malik is taken as a vocative, iyyāka continues address rather than making an iltifāt; shifts to third person can nevertheless follow a vocative, as the cited poems show.
rows.anchor: ومن ذهب إلى أن ملك منادى

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī counts three iltifāts in Imruʾ al-Qays’s lines, but Abū Ḥayyān identifies only two: address to third person, then third person to first person.
rows.anchor: ودعوى الزمخشري في أبيات امرئ القيس الثلاثة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān rejects identifying the first shift by inferred presence: iltifāt concerns actual wording, and inserting an unspoken say before either phrase would remove the shift.
rows.anchor: إن الأول هو الانتقال من الغيبة إلى الحضور أشد خطأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passive reading iyyāka yuʿbadu seems to lack a governor for the accusative pronoun; Abū Ḥayyān explains it as a metaphorical substitution of nominative anta, followed by an unusual shift to third person.
rows.anchor: وقراءة من قرأ إياك يعبد بالياء مبنياً للمفعول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worship can also mean obedience, as in the command not to worship Satan.
rows.anchor: أو الطاعة ، كقوله تعالى : { لا تعبد الشيطان }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some interpret worship here as drawing near to God through obedience.
rows.anchor: أو التقرب بالطاعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worship is also interpreted as supplication, as in the warning against those who disdain worship.
rows.anchor: أو الدعاء أن الذين يستكبرون عن عبادتي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worship is also explained as affirming God's oneness, as in the statement that jinn and humankind were created only to worship.
rows.anchor: التوحيد إلا ليعبدون أي ليوحدون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The meanings offered for worship—humility, obedience, drawing near, supplication, and affirming oneness—are close in sense.
rows.anchor: وفسرت العبادة في إياك نعبد بأنها التذلل والخضوع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joining worship to seeking help combines what the servant offers God with what the servant asks from Him.
rows.anchor: وقرنت الاستعانة بالعبادة للجمع بين ما يتقرب به العبد إلى الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worship precedes the request for aid because the means is presented before the need, so the request may be answered.
rows.anchor: وقدمت العبادة على الاستعانة لتقديم الوسيلة قبل طلب الحاجة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unqualified terms worship and seeking help encompass every act of worship and every matter for which help is sought.
rows.anchor: وأطلق العبادة والاستعانة لتتناول كل معبود به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeating iyyāka makes worship and seeking help two independently intended sentences.
rows.anchor: وكرر إياك ليكون كل من العبادة والاستعانة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated iyyāka explicitly identifies God as the one from whom aid is sought; without it, the wording could leave the source unspecified.
rows.anchor: وللتنصيص على طلب العون منه

rows.speaker: بعض المنتمين للصلاح
rows.claim: Some pious interpreters restrict worship to knowledge and seeking help to gnosis, but Abū Ḥayyān says the wording gives no evidence for these restrictions.
rows.anchor: ونقل عن المنتمين للصلاح تقييدات مختلفة

rows.speaker: قالوا
rows.claim: They say naʿbud refutes the determinists while nastaʿīn refutes the Qadarites.
rows.anchor: وفي قوله : نعبد قالوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worship is an exalted station, commanded in scripture and used as an honorific for the most excellent creatures, including the Prophet and Jesus.
rows.anchor: ومقام العبادة شريف ، وقد جاء الأمر به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse God gives in 20:14 places worship after exclusive monotheism, because monotheism is the foundation and worship its branch.
rows.anchor: لأن التوحيد هو الأصل ، والعبادة فرعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Directly addressing God as present refutes materialists, atheists, and those who deny a creator.
rows.anchor: وقالوا في قوله : إياك . رد على الدهرية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hadā can mean guiding, directing, leading ahead, or making something clear; it can also mean inspiration or calling, depending on context.
rows.anchor: الإرشاد والدلالة والتقدم ومنه الهوادي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording about Thamūd is an example of guidance meaning clarification.
rows.anchor: وأما ثمود فهديناهم

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: The commentators explain that God inspired all animals toward what benefits them in the verse about giving each thing its creation and guidance.
rows.anchor: معناه ألهم الحيوانات كلها إلى منافعها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the phrase every people has a guide, guide means a caller or preacher.
rows.anchor: ولكل قوم هاد أي داع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb hadā originally takes its second object with li- or ilā; usage broadened to take it directly, as in ihdinā al-ṣirāṭ.
rows.anchor: ثم يتسع فيه فيعدى إليه بنفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The nūn in ihdinā can represent the speaker together with others, or be the plural of majesty.
rows.anchor: ون ضمير المتكلم ومعه غيره أو معظم نفسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ṣirāṭ means the road or path.
rows.anchor: وأصله بالسين من السرط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The original form begins with sīn and derives from saraṭ, swallowing; the road is named as though it swallows what travels it.
rows.anchor: وأصله بالسين من السرط

rows.speaker: قنبل ورويس
rows.claim: Qunbul and Ruways read the original form with sīn.
rows.anchor: وبالسين على الأصل قرأ قبل ورويس

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Replacing sīn with ṣād is the standard Qurashī form; the majority read it, and it is the spelling in the codex.
rows.anchor: وإبدال سينه صاداً هي الفصحى ، وهي لغة قريش

rows.speaker: الأصمعي عن أبي عمرو
rows.claim: Al-Aṣmaʿī reports a zāy pronunciation from Abū ʿAmr.
rows.anchor: وزايا لغة رواها الأصمعي عن أبي عمرو

rows.speaker: حمزة
rows.claim: A sound between zāy and ṣād is a Qays dialect; Ḥamza reads it with variants and detail among his transmitters.
rows.anchor: وأشمامها زاياً لغة قيس ، وبه قرأ حمزة

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abū ʿAlī reports sīn, ṣād, and an intermediate zāy-ṣād pronunciation from Abū ʿAmr; al-ʿAryān transmits it through Abū Sufyān, and al-Aṣmaʿī reports a pure zāy.
rows.anchor: أبو علي : وروي عن أبي عمرو

rows.speaker: بعض اللغويين
rows.claim: Some linguists accuse al-Aṣmaʿī of mistaking an intermediate pronunciation for a pure zāy; Abū ʿAlī attributes this criticism to Ibn Mujāhid.
rows.anchor: بعض اللغويين : ما حكاه الأصمعي

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر الطوسي
rows.claim: Al-Ṭūsī says ṣād is Qurashī and good Arabic, sīn is common among Arabs, and zāy belongs to ʿUdhra, Kaʿb, and Banū al-Qayn.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو جعفر الطوسي في تفسيره ، وهو إمام من أئمة الإمامية : الصراط بالصاد لغة قريش

rows.speaker: أبو بكر بن مجاهد
rows.claim: Ibn Mujāhid says the intermediate zāy-ṣād reading is an awkwardly produced sound between two letters, not one of the alphabetic phonemes.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو بكر بن مجاهد ، وهذه القراءة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān does not deny that the intermediate sound belongs to eloquent Arab speech, but judges ṣād more eloquent and widespread.
rows.anchor: إلا أن الصاد أفصح وأوسع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ṣirāṭ can be masculine or feminine, with masculine usage more frequent.
rows.anchor: إلا أن الصاد أفصح وأوسع ، ويذكر ويؤنث

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر الطوسي
rows.claim: Al-Ṭūsī says Hijaz speakers treat ṣirāṭ like other path and place nouns as feminine, while Tamīm speakers make them masculine.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو جعفر الطوسي : أهل الحجاز يؤنثون الصراط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If ṣirāṭ is masculine its common plural is suruṭ and its small plural is asriṭa; if feminine, its plural pattern is afʿul, as with dhirāʿ/adruʿ and shimāl/ashmul.
rows.anchor: ويجمع في الكثرة على سرط

rows.speaker: زيد بن علي، والضحاك، ونصر بن علي عن الحسن
rows.claim: Zayd ibn ʿAlī, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and Naṣr ibn ʿAlī from al-Ḥasan read an indefinite ṣirāṭan mustaqīman without the definite article, as in the cited passage.
rows.anchor: وقرأ زيد بن علي ، والضحاك ، ونصر بن علي ، عن الحسن : اهدنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mustaqīm derives from istaqāma, where istifʿala has the simple verb sense of qāma: to stand upright without bending.
rows.anchor: والقيام هو الانتصاب والاستواء من غير اعوجاج
